steps.body: Three strange facts. **×1 keeps**: one group of 8 is just 8. **×0 empties**: 8 groups of nothing is 0. **÷1 keeps too**: share 8 with only 1 person and they get all 8. They're easy — but sneaky, because the +1 and +0 rules whisper wrong answers.
The trap, exposed one panel at a time.

panels.title: 5 × 1 keeps
panels.body: 5 × 1 means five groups with 1 in each: five things in all. Multiplying by 1 changes nothing — the number keeps itself.

panels.title: 5 × 0 empties
panels.body: 5 × 0 means five groups with NOTHING in each: 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0. Five empty bags still hold zero.

panels.title: The trap
panels.body: 5 + 0 = 5 because adding nothing keeps your pile. But 5 × 0 makes your pile INTO nothings — 0. Adding nothing keeps; multiplying by nothing empties.

widget.continueFeedback: Keep revealing — the trap springs in the last panel.
widget.successFeedback: That's the whole trick: +0 keeps the pile, ×0 replaces it with empty groups.

steps.body: Only one of these survives the strange-facts test.
explanationVariants: One group of 7 is 7 — multiplying by 1 keeps the number exactly as it is.
7 × 1 builds a single group holding 7. Nothing gets added, nothing gets emptied: still 7.

options.feedback: One group of 7 is 7. Times one always keeps the number.
That's the +0 rule sneaking in. Adding 0 keeps 7, but 7 × 0 makes seven EMPTY groups — 0.
It kept the wrong number! One group OF 7 holds 7 things — the 7 survives, not the 1.
Flipping never rescues a zero — zero groups of 7 is as empty as 7 groups of zero. Both are 0.

steps.body: Division has strange ones too. **9 ÷ 1 = 9**: one person gets the whole pile. **9 ÷ 9 = 1**: nine people share nine things — one each. Different questions, so don't swap them: ÷1 keeps the number, ÷itself gives 1.
Zero doesn't care how big the other number is.
explanationVariants: 398 groups with nothing in each is still nothing: 0 + 0 + … + 0 = 0, no matter how many zeros line up.
×0 empties every time — even a number in the hundreds becomes 0 the moment its groups are empty.

commonErrors.feedback: 398 is what ×1 (or +0) would give. But these 398 groups are EMPTY — count nothing 398 times and you hold nothing.
3980 glues a zero on, as if this were ×10 shifting the number. Multiplying BY zero doesn't attach a digit; it empties the whole thing.
399 adds 1. Neither +1 nor +0 is happening here — ×0 turns any pile, however huge, into 0.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Ask what the groups hold: 398 groups of nothing. Adding up nothings — even 398 of them — gives 0.

steps.body: Move from zero groups of 6 to one group of 6.

widget.prompt: Start with 0 groups of 6, then slide to make 1 group of 6. Watch the total change from 0 to 6.
widget.lowFeedback: At 0 groups, there are no dots: 6 × 0 = 0. Move to 1 group.
widget.successFeedback: One group has 6 dots, while zero groups has none. So 1 × 6 = 6 and 0 × 6 = 0.

predict.prompt: Do 0 groups of 6 and 1 group of 6 have the same total?
predict.reveal: Zero groups contain no dots, so 0 × 6 = 0. One group contains 6 dots, so 1 × 6 = 6. The totals are different.

steps.body: Spot the strange fact working inside a story.
explanationVariants: Each coin gives exactly 1 sticker, so 8 coins give 8 × 1 = 8 stickers.
Eight groups with 1 sticker in each: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 8.

widget.prompt: A sticker machine gives 1 sticker per coin. Zoe puts in 8 coins. Which fact counts her stickers?

options.feedback: Eight coins, one sticker each: 8 × 1 = 8. Times one keeps the count of coins.
×0 would mean the machine gives NOTHING per coin — poor Zoe! This machine pays 1 each time.
That adds one extra sticker on top of the coins. Each coin trades for exactly one sticker — the counts match at 8.
That's one coin's story. Zoe fed the machine 8 coins — eight groups of 1.

steps.body: A shorter riddle first — two moves instead of three.
explanationVariants: Multiplying by 1 is a do-nothing step — 12 stays 12 — so the whole riddle is really just 12+3=15.

widget.prompt: A shorter riddle: start with 12. Multiply by 1. Then add 3. What number do you have now?

commonErrors.feedback: 13 treats ×1 like it adds 1 — it doesn't. ×1 leaves 12 exactly as it is; then +3 gives 15.
36 is 12×3, as if the riddle said ×3 instead of ×1 then +3. Multiplying by 1 changes nothing: 12, then +3=15.

widget.fallbackFeedback: ×1 does nothing to 12 — it's still 12. Then just add 3: 12+3=15.

steps.body: A number riddle with a trap in the middle.
hints: Follow the steps one at a time, left to right — don't skip any.
47 × 1 = 47. Now the trap: what does 47 × 0 make?
Anything × 0 is 0. So you're holding 0 — now add the 5.
explanationVariants: The ×0 in the middle erases everything before it — only the final +5 survives.

widget.prompt: A riddle: start with 47. Multiply by 1. Multiply the result by 0. Then add 5. What number do you have now?

commonErrors.feedback: 52 is 47 + 5 — the ×0 step got skipped! It empties the pile to 0 before the 5 arrives.
47 treats ×0 like ×1 or +0 — as if it keeps the number. ×0 empties it, and then there's still a +5 to do.
0 is right after the ×0 trap — nearly there! One step remains: add 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Do each step in order: ×1 keeps 47, ×0 empties it to 0, then +5.

steps.body: The strange ones can't sneak up on you now.
takeaways: ×1 and ÷1 keep the number exactly as it is.
Anything × 0 is 0 — in either order, no matter how big.
Don't let +0 and +1 habits leak into × problems.
steps.teaser: chapter 3 turns you fast — doubles, fives, tens, and the sneaky nines pattern.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Ask what's IN the groups. 3 × 1: three groups holding 1 each — three things. 3 × 0: three groups holding **nothing** — zero things. Multiplying by 0 always empties, because empty groups add up to empty.

explanationVariants: ×0 empties any number — the 3 groups have nothing inside.

options.feedback: Three groups of nothing is nothing: 0.
3 is what +0 (or ×1) keeps. But ×0 makes the groups empty — the 3 has nothing to count.
30 glues a zero on, as if this were ×10 shifting 3 into 30. ×0 doesn't attach a digit; it empties the pile.
